query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A multifunctional, gradient surface coating deposited via physical vapor deposition (PVD) that incorporates a high-temperature–stable lubricious oxide multilayer will enable the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy to maintain low friction and reduced wear across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a multifunctional, gradient surface coating by PVD to form a lubricious oxide-based multilayer structure
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient air with a moderate normal load (≈10 N) over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, ensuring exposure to oxidation and thermal cycling
generation.structural_mediator: A gradient, multilayer oxide structure that forms a robust and self-adaptive tribo-film at the sliding interface
generation.mechanism: Under friction, the engineered multilayer coating gradually develops a stable lubricious oxide film that compensates for temperature-induced degradation mechanisms (e.g., excessive oxidation or thermal softening) in the substrate. This self-adaptive tribo-film reduces shear strength at the interface, thereby lowering the friction coefficient and wear rate compared with the uncoated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated CoCrFeNi specimen will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range compared to the uncoated baseline, with performance maintained even at high temperatures (up to 800 °C).
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi alloy without any surface coating
generation.boundary: Temperature: room temperature to 800 °C; Load: moderate (~10 N); Environment: ambient air; Sliding conditions that incorporate oxidation and thermal cycling effects
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in friction coefficient and wear rate is uncertain and may be influenced by coating thickness, layer composition, and microstructural uniformity achieved during PVD processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set with the applied gradient lubricious oxide multilayer coating via PVD and one set uncoated. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled conditions (load ≈10 N, temperatures incrementally increasing from room temperature to 800 °C, in ambient air).
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) as a function of temperature
Wear rate (mass loss or wear volume) across the temperature range
Surface morphology and oxide layer integrity via SEM/EDS analysis post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the uncoated samples across the full temperature range, or if the coating fails to form a continuous, stable oxide lubricious layer under the testing conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study prepares Ni50(AlNbTiV)50-xY2O3 complex concentrated alloy composite coatings and analyzes their microstructure, phase composition, and high-temperature performance. The results indicate that each coating is composed of FCC phases, including γ-FeNi, Ni3Al, and Ni3(Al, Ti), as well as BCC phases such as Ni3Nb and Ni3Ti. With increasing Y2O3 content, the lamellar structure in the inter-dendritic regions of the coatings first decreases and then increases. The wear mechanism of the coating without Y2O3 addition under high-temperature conditions involves the combined effects of abrasive wear and adhesive wear. The coating with a 0.6 wt.% addition exhibits the smallest cracks and the lowest oxidation rate in high-temperature oxidation and thermal shock tests, with the oxidation weight gain reduced by 26.2% compared to the coating without Y2O3 addition. The abrasive and adhesive wear of this coating is mitigated, and the average friction coefficient and mass loss are decreased. When the mass fraction of Y2O3 is 0.4 wt.%, the coating structure shows a significant refinement effect and exhibits the best performance in tensile strength and high-temperature friction and wear tests.

Both sliding speed and normal load will affect the friction and wear behavior of the different grain size CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Increasing the sliding speed will increase the friction coefficient and specific wear rate of the alloy. Thus, increase the normal load, reduce the friction coefficient, and decrease the specific wear rate of the alloy. This is because the oxide layer formed on the worn surface under high load plays a role in lubrication and reduces the friction coefficient and specific wear rate.

chosen.lever: application of a multifunctional, gradient surface coating
chosen.technique: physical vapor deposition (PVD) of a multilayered lubricious oxide coating
chosen.conditions: Testing under sliding conditions from room temperature to 800 °C, at moderate loads (≈10 N) in ambient air, where the coating is engineered to maintain a low friction coefficient and resist wear through the formation of a robust, self-adaptive tribo‐film.
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the identified performance limitation by compensating for the degradation mechanisms (e.g., oxidation and thermal instability) that challenge the CoCrFeNi matrix over a wide temperature range. Prior studies have demonstrated that surface coatings—particularly multilayer or gradient oxide films deposited via PVD—can reliably reduce the coefficient of friction and wear under both low- and high-temperature sliding conditions. The proposed controlled falsification experiment (comparing coated and uncoated samples under identical variable conditions) will allow for the isolation of the coating’s effect on friction and wear, thereby providing a decisive test of the hypothesis.
